region.zh: 美國喬治亞中部種植園地帶

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus' (2024 print of 1883), tale XXVII 'Brother Wolf Says Grace'

summary.en: Caught in a trap with Brer Wolf's jaws closing, Brer Rabbit plays the etiquette-master: show your politeness, Brer Wolf — fold your hands under your chin, shut your eyes, and say grace — 'Bless us and blind us, and put us in the crack where the Ole Boy can't find us' — and before the blessing is finished, the wiggled-for rabbit lights on his feet and leaves a blue streak behind him.
summary.zh: 被狼咬住之際，兔哥哥扮起禮儀導師：『狼兄，展現你的教養——合掌於頷、閉目謝恩：願我們蒙福又致盲，藏進那老魔頭找不到的石縫』——祝禱未畢，兔仔一扭落地，身後只留一道藍煙。

sensitivity.note: Brer Rabbit cycle; grace-trick amusement tale. Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: Caught with Brer Wolf closing in, Brer Rabbit asked how he could show his politeness: 'I want you to say grace, Brer Wolf, and say it quick, because I am getting mighty weak. Fold your hands under your chin, Brer Wolf, and shut your eyes, and say: Bless us and blind us, and put us in the crack where the Ole Boy can't find us. Say it quick, Brer Wolf, because I am failing mighty fast.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XXVII (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Brer Wolf put up his hands and shot his eyes and began, 'Bless us and blind us' — but he did not get any farther: just as he took up his hands, Brer Rabbit fetched a wiggle, lit on his feet, and left a blue streak behind him. 'Oh, I just knew Brother Rabbit would get away!' the little boy declared; and Uncle Remus said that was right — put your dependence in Brer Rabbit and you won't be far out of the way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XXVII, ending (1883); not verbatim.

title.en: Spirits, Seen and Unseen: Daddy Jack's Ghost-Lore
title.zh: 顯形與隱形的靈：傑克老爹的鬼譚

region.en: Middle Georgia plantation country, USA (Daddy Jack, a Congo-born teller)
region.zh: 美國喬治亞中部種植園（講述者傑克老爹，剛果出生）

texts.period: African-American oral tradition (Congo and Georgia tellers); collected 1879-1881; published 2024 (published 1883)

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus' (2024 print of 1883), tale XXVIII 'Spirits, Seen and Unseen'

summary.en: Congo-born Daddy Jack holds forth on the dead: children who laugh and talk to empty corners see ha'nts; a spirit called his name across the creek and his uncle walking backward by sundown proved it; and the Jack-me-Lantern — the dead man's ghost hunting the money that was stolen from him — can only be turned by turning your coat inside out, if you can get the sleeve turned. In the paired witch-lore, the old witch leaves her skin drying by the fire, finds it shrunk and stinking and no longer fits, and a black wolf lies in the yard by the fire's light.
summary.zh: 剛果出生的傑克老爹縱談鬼神：對著空角嬉笑自語的孩子，是見了鬼；溪對岸呼名的精靈，由日落倒行的叔父作證；『傑克燈』——被害者的亡靈持燈尋找被奪的錢財——唯把外套反穿方能退之。女巫篇：老巫離體而去的皮掛在火邊晾曬，尋回時已縮臭不合身；火光照見院中臥著一頭黑狼。

sensitivity.note: Ghost-lore and witch-lore discussion among named African-American tellers (Daddy Jack born in Africa; Aunt Tempy, Uncle Remus); transcribed 1879-1881. This is folklore conversation, not ritual instruction; no conjure recipes beyond the folklore-level witch-test ('double, double, double up!') recorded by Harris.

passages.text: Aunt Tempy came in feeling mighty creepy: setting up in her house a while ago, she heard Riah's little girl talking in the other room — and found the child sitting flat in the middle of the floor, laughing and talking and making motions like she saw somebody in the corner, asking them to stay on their own side, and threatening to get a switch and drive them back. 'They tell me,' said Uncle Remus, 'that when you hear children talking and going on so plainly with themselves, they are bound to see ha'nts.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XXVIII (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Daddy Jack roused himself: 'You no bin-a see dem ghos'? I is bin-a see plenty ghos'; I no 'fraid dem; I is bin-a punch dem 'way wit' me cane.' Once, when he was a young man going for water and dipping his piggin under the creek, he heard a voice call him — Jack! O Jack! — and Titty Ann swore she had not called: dead ghos' is bin-a call. He raised his eyes and saw his nuncle going by sundown, going backward, and when folks came to fetch the old man out, he had been taken with the hiccup, throwing his head this way and that — 'I is bin-a see mo' dead ghos', but me no spot um lak dis.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XXVIII, middle (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Of the Jack-me-Lantern, Daddy Jack told how, making his way through thick swamp, hot and cold, his back quaking and his breath coming fast, he saw the light making its way through the bush, coming straight by him, flick-flickering, close and closer. The old folks' talk was to turn your coat-sleeve when the Jack-me-Lantern runs you; he pulled and twisted and yerked at the jacket, but it had grown on his back — until he said his prayer upon it, and the sleeve turned. The Jack-me-Lantern saw it, lifted up, said Phew! and was gone: 'You no walk in the swamp 'cep' you keep your coat across the arm.' Aunt Tempy had heard tell that this Jacky-ma-Lantern was a sure-enough spirit — a man who got killed, whose money folks took; now his ha'nt has gone and got a light to hunt up where his money is, and spirits don't walk and walk less they got something on their mind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XXVIII, middle-b (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Asked whether witches were spirits, Daddy Jack — proud of his reputation as a witch — answered that a witch is no dead ghost but living folks you shake hands with, and told the heifer test: when the moon is shining low, wet your hand with pot-licker grease, rub a young heifer's nose, get on her back, hold her by the ear, gallop down the lane till you come to a big gully, and holler 'Double, double, double up!' — if the heifer jumps, you are a witch; if not, no witch. And of the old witch who leaves her skin where she starts from: a man passing found the green skin drying by the fire, hung it up till it shrunk and swiveled and stank, and pitched it in the yard — and when the witch came hunting for her skin, she tried it on this way and that way and it would not fit, and she cried 'Skin! Don't you know me?' while the skin said nothing at all, and the big black wolf lay by the skin in the yard with his teeth showing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XXVIII, ending (1883); not verbatim.

title.en: Brother Rabbit and His Famous Foot

region.zh: 美國喬治亞中部種植園地帶

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus' (2024 print of 1883), tale XXX 'Brother Rabbit and His Famous Foot'

summary.en: Uncle Remus's rabbit's-foot charm and its origin tale: so much luck attending Brer Rabbit that the creatures concluded he carried a conjure-bag — a natural-born witch, or in cahoots with one — and resolved to make up with him to find out how come he was so lucky. The answer went round in the women's talk and the men's prying, and the hind foot stayed with the lucky one; whosoever carries it comes out the right end of every racket, and a rabbit crossing the road must be crossed out with a spit-marked cross in the sand.
summary.zh: 雷慕斯老人的兔腳護符及其來歷：兔哥哥運氣太旺，群獸斷定他身懷咒物——或是天生的巫者，或與巫勾結——遂決計向他示好打聽根由。答案在女人們的閒談與男人們的窺探之間流轉，那隻後腳便永遠伴著幸運兒；攜它者逢凶化吉，兔過大路須以唾畫十字將運氣截住。

sensitivity.note: Hoodoo-charm origin tale at folklore level (lucky rabbit-foot; road-cross counter-ritual recorded as folk practice). Harris collected these from named Georgia tellers; the charm is discussed as folk belief, not instruction.

passages.text: Uncle Remus's rabbit's hind foot, a very large one, was for keeping off boogers. 'When I had to run errands for myself all times of night, and take nigh cuts through the woods, and across by the burying-ground, it is monstrously handy to have that rabbit foot. If there was any boogers, and they came slinking after me, they would find out directly that the old nigger was heeled with a rabbit foot.' A strip of red flannel tied round your arm would keep off the rheumatis; stump-water would cure the fever; some good for one disease and some for another — but the point is that the rabbit foot gives good luck: the man that carries it is mighty apt to come out right-end up when there is any racket going on in the neighborhoods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XXX (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: When a rabbit runs across the big road in front of him, Uncle Remus does not shoo at it or make to kill it — he squats right down in the middle of the road, makes a cross-mark in the sand, and spits in it. 'When rabbit crosses your luck, what you going do, unless you set down and cross it out, right then and there?' People who shoot rabbits in the big road, he noticed, do not come to any good end. How people found out about the rabbit's foot: the women do the talking and the flying, the men do the walking and the prying, and betwixt and between them there is not much that does not come out — if it does not come out one day it does the next.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XXX, middle (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the days when Brer Rabbit was keeping the neighborhoods stirred up, the other creatures studied and studied the whole blessed time how they were going to nab him. When all their plans, and their traps, and their jugglements did no good, they all agreed that Brer Rabbit had some conjurement he tricked them with: Brer Bear allowed he was bound to be a natural-born witch; Brer Wolf said he suspected Brer Rabbit was just in cahoots with a witch; Brer Fox vowed he had more luck than smartness. Day in and day out they worked with the puzzlement, and sat up nights, until they agreed among themselves that they had better make up with Brer Rabbit and see if they could not find out how come he was so lucky — and while all this was going on, ole Brer Rabbit was galloping round from Funtown to Frolicville, kicking up the devilment and terrifying the neighborhoods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XXX, ending (1883); not verbatim.

region.zh: 美國喬治亞中部種植園地帶

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus' (2024 print of 1883), tale XLII 'The Fire-Test' (told by Aunt Tempy and Uncle Remus)

summary.en: Brer Wolf, eavesdropping behind the house, steals the family password — 'I'll stay when you are away, because no gold will pay toll' — and after two botched attempts learns to sing it fine, opens the door, and gobbles the little Rabs up, leaving only a pile of bones in the swept clean corner. Judge Terrapin convenes the settlement, digs a deep pit, fills it with lightwood knots, kindles it high, and declares the child-destroyer will drop in and be burnt up at the trial jump; Mink and Coon sail over, Bear pants across, and the boastful digger-and-filler-and-kindler takes his long running start, jumps, squalls, and drops right spang in the middle of the fire.
summary.zh: 狼哥哥屋後偷聽，竊得家門口令——『你們不在家我也守著，因為黃金不付過路錢』——兩番碰壁後苦練歌喉，唱得字正腔圓，開門吞盡小兔一家，爐邊只剩一堆骨。龜法官召集全鄉，掘深坑、填松節、燃高火，宣告殺童者過火必墜；貂與浣熊一躍而過，熊氣喘吁吁也能跨——偏偏那個又挖又填又點火的誇口者，助跑太長力氣用盡，一躍慘叫，正正落在火焰中央。

sensitivity.note: Password-fire-trial tale (ATU 123-linked wolf-and-kids cycle, US variant). Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: When Brer Rabbit got ready to go off for a mess of green truck, he called all his children up and told them that when he went out they must fasten the door on the inside and not turn anybody in, nohow, because Brer Fox and Brer Wolf had been lying round waiting a chance to nab him; and when he came back, he would rap at the door and sing: 'I'll stay when you are away, because no gold will pay toll!' The little Rabs held up their hands and promised not to open the door for nobody except their daddy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XLII (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: But all this time Brer Wolf had been hiding out behind the house, and he heard every word that passed; and before Brer Rabbit was out of sight, Brer Wolf went to the door and knocked — blip, blip, blip! — and sang the song. The little Rabs laughed fit to kill themselves: 'Go away, Mr. Wolf, go away! You are not any of we-all daddy!' He slunk off, but every time he thought of those plump little Rabs he got hungrier; the second attempt failed — 'we-all daddy has not got no bad cold like that' — and the third: 'we-all daddy can sing lots prettier than that.' So he went away out in the woods and sang, and sang, till he could sing fine as the next man, went back and knocked, and sang so nice and sang so fine that they undid the door — and ole Brer Wolf walked in and gobbled them all up, from the first to the last. When ole Brer Rabbit got home he found the door standing wide open and all the children gone: no sign of any tussle, the hearth all swept clean, everything all to rights — but right over in the corner he saw a pile of bones, and then he knew in reason that some of the other creatures had been there and made hash out of his children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XLII, middle (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: He laid the case before Brer Tarrypin, who was a mighty man in those days; no sooner did he hear the state of the condition than he called all the creatures together and allowed that the man who destroyed Brer Rabbit's children must be caught, or there was no telling how long it would be before the same somebody came along and destroyed all the children in the settlement. 'Less dig a deep pit.' — 'I'll dig the pit,' said Brer Wolf. 'Less fill the pit full of lightered knots and brush.' — 'I'll fill the pit,' said Brer Wolf. 'Now, less set it a-fire.' — 'I'll kindle the fire,' said Brer Wolf. When the fire began to blaze up, Brer Tarrypin declared the creatures must jump across it, and the man who destroyed Brer Rabbit's children would drop in and get burnt up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XLII, ending (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Brer Wolf had been so uppity about digging, and filling, and kindling, that they all expected him to make the first trial — but, bless your soul and body! Brer Wolf looked like he had some other business to attend to. The pit looked so deep and the fire burnt so high that they most all feared to make the trial; Brer Mink made a running start and lit across, Brer Coon sailed over, Brer Bear panted across saying he was heavier than he had ever been in all his born days but never hurted Brer Rabbit's poor little children — until it came Brer Wolf's time. Then he began to get scared, and was mighty sorry he dug that pit so deep and wide and kindled that fire so high; he took such a long running start that when he got to the jumping place he was done wo' teetotally out, and he lit up, fetched a squall, and dropped right spang in the middle of the fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XLII, ending (1883); not verbatim.

title.en: The Cunning Snake: Coomba and the Song-Password
title.zh: 狡蛇記：庫姆巴與歌之口令

region.en: Congo (Daddy Jack's telling) recalled on a Georgia plantation, USA
region.zh: 剛果（傑克老爹講述）回憶於喬治亞種植園

texts.period: African oral tradition (Congo teller); collected 1879-1881; published 2024 (published 1883)

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus' (2024 print of 1883), tale XLIII 'The Cunning Snake' (told by Daddy Jack, an African-born teller)

summary.en: Daddy Jack's African sing-tale: Coomba, hungry in dream for the big snake's eggs, eats them for breakfast; the mother snake tracks her by scent and warns — take care your own. The song-password 'Walla walla witto, me Noncy' with the answer 'Andolee! Andoli! Andolo!' keeps the baby safe until the snake, coiled in the chimney corner holding its breath for days, learns the call; the door opens, the snake swallows Noncy whole, and the mother follows the track into the swamp, breaks the sleeper's head with a cane, cuts her open, and washes the living child — who wakes answering the song.
summary.zh: 傑克老爹的非洲歌謠：庫姆巴夢中思蛋成癡，將大蛇之卵煮作早餐；蛇母循跡而至，留下警言——看好你自己的孩子。歌之口令『瓦拉瓦拉維托，我的南西』與應答『安多利！安多利！安多羅！』守護嬰兒多日，直到蛇在煙囪角屏息學會呼喚；門開，整孩吞下。母親循跡入沼，以杖擊碎睡蛇之頭、剖腹取女、洗淨抱回——孩子睜眼便應著那支歌。

sensitivity.note: Song-password tale told by Daddy Jack, an African-born (Congo) teller, in his African creole; a rare trans-Atlantic witness of the password cycle. Dialect preserved conceptually, rendered to standard English in paraphrase; songs kept as transcribed formulae.

passages.text: One time there was one old Affiky ooman, her name was Coomba. She went walking through the woods and through the field, and by and by came upon a snake-nest full of eggs — a big snake, big eggs. The Affiky woman wanted those eggs so bad; she was afraid to take them, went home, saw them in her dream, wanted them so bad; and the next morning she said she must have them. She went out, found the snake-nest, got the eggs, carried them to her own house, and cooked them for her breakfast.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XLIII (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: By and by the snake came to its nest: the eggs were gone. It put its nose on the ground and tracked the woman by her own house, and asked about the eggs; she said she had not seen any eggs, though the snake saw the skin that had been on them and asked what this was — and she said nothing at all. 'Woman! You have heard my voice when I cried out. You have taken my eggs; you have destroyed my children. Take care of your own; take care of your own.' The snake went away, slicked out its tongue, slid away. The woman had a pretty little pickaninny she loved hard all over; mindful of what the snake said, she carried the child round on her back, called her Noncy, carried her far, loved her hard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XLIII, middle (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: The snake stayed in the bush-side, watched all day, waited all night, and got hungry for the pickaninny — and the woman, carrying Noncy until she was tired, puffed and blew and worked her gills like a catfish, then put the child down and made up a song in her head and taught the little girl to answer it, and showed her how to pull out the peg in the door: put the peg in and open for nobody except you hear me sing. When she started off she sang, 'Walla walla witto, me Noncy!' — and the little girl answered, 'Andolee! Andoli! Andolo!' — and pulled out the peg, and ran to her mother. Day after day it was the same, while the snake lay coiled up in the bush, watching the night, listening by day, trying to learn the song and saying nothing at all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XLIII, middle-b (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: One time when the mother was away, the snake waited till it was almost time for her to come back, went by the door, opened its mouth and sang — 'Wullo wullo widdo, me Noncy!' — trying to make its voice come fine like the little girl's mother, but there was a rough place in its throat and the voice came big: 'Go away from here! My mother does not holler the song like that!' It tried one, two, three times — no use; the little girl did not open the door, and the snake said it must learn the song for sure. It coiled up in the chimney corner and held its breath to listen; all day long it thought about the song, said it forward, said it backward, and at most toward sundown it came at the door and hollered the song fine — and the little girl, thinking the snake was her mother, answered the song and opened the door quick, and ran upon the snake before she saw it: the snake hugged the little girl more like than her mother, twisted its tail round her, squeezed her tight, and swallowed her whole, breaking no bone. The mother came home, hollered the song and got no answer, and her voice shook and her body trembled; she looked all round, saw where the snake had crossed the road, cut a cane in the swamp, followed the track, and came upon the snake lying asleep — took the cane and broke its head, mashed it flat, cut the snake open, and found the little girl just like she was asleep; took her home and washed her off, and by and by the little girl opened her eyes and, soon as she saw her mother, answered the song: 'Andolee! Andoli! Andolo!' — and she was alive. Enty!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XLIII, ending (1883); not verbatim.

region.en: Middle Georgia plantation country, USA (symbolic pin: the creek that became the ocean)
region.zh: 美國喬治亞中部種植園（象徵定位：化作大洋的小溪）

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus' (2024 print of 1883), tale LVIII 'The Origin of the Ocean'

summary.en: A hunting camp etiology: every prize Mr. Lion brings down is claimed — 'it's mine! I killed it!' — while Rabbit does the actual shooting. Around the night fire Rabbit engineers a prank of cold ashes and hot embers, blaming sleepers across the creek, until the bellowing Lion leaps the water to avenge the insult; then Brer Rabbit cuts the string that holds the banks together, the banks keep falling back, the creek keeps widening, and from that day to this the big waters have been rolling between them — which is why the lions and all the servigous creatures live on the other side.
summary.zh: 獵營之夜的起源故事：獅子每奪一獵便喊『是我的！是我打死的！』——其實槍槍都是兔子放的。夜火旁，兔仔設下冷灰與熱炭的惡作劇，誣指溪對岸的搗亂者，引得獅子長吼躍溪報仇；兔仔趁機割斷縛住兩岸的繩索——河岸不斷崩退，溪水不斷變寬，直到兩造彼此不復相見——自此大水橫亙，獅子與所有兇獸都住在那一邊。

sensitivity.note: Origin-of-the-ocean etiology from the Brer Rabbit cycle; flood-cluster record (cross-ref: norse, hebrew, mesopotamian flood records). Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: One time way back yonder, before there were any folks fooling round, Mr. Lion took a notion that he would go hunting, and nothing would do him but Brer Rabbit must go with him. Brer Rabbit allowed he was up for any kind of fun on the top side of the ground; they put out and hunted clean across the country — and every time Mr. Lion let loose and missed the game, Brer Rabbit let loose and fetched it down, and no sooner did he do that than Mr. Lion squalled out, 'It's mine! It's mine! I killed it!' Mr. Lion was such a big man that Brer Rabbit was scared to dispute along with him, but he laid it up in his mind to get even with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale LVIII (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: They hunted all day long, and when night came they were so far from home that they had to camp out; they came to a creek, scraped away the trash, built a fire on the bank, and cooked their supper. After supper they sat up telling tales, and Brer Rabbit bragged about what a good hunter Mr. Lion was; when their eyelids got heavy, Rabbit warned that he was a monstrous heavy sleeper, and asked Mr. Lion to show him how he snored before he got sound asleep — and after he was sound asleep. Mr. Lion sucked in his breath, and every time he sucked in his breath it sounded like a whole passel of mules whinnying after fodder.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale LVIII, middle (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Brer Rabbit heard that snore he got up, sprinkled himself with the cold ashes round the fire, and flung a whole passel of hot embers on Mr. Lion, who jumped up and asked who did that; Brer Rabbit lay there kicking at his ear with his behind foot and hollering Ow! — the ashes on his own hide puzzling the Lion. Twice more the same doings happened, and the second time Brer Rabbit hollered, 'I seed um, Mr. Lion! I seed the way they come from 'cross the creek! They most sho'ly did!' — and Mr. Lion fetched a bellow and jumped across the creek. No sooner did he do that than Brer Rabbit cut the string that held the banks together, and, lo and behold, there they were: the banks fell back, the creek kept getting wider and wider, until Brer Rabbit and Mr. Lion were not in sight of one another, and from that day to this the big waters have been rolling between them — we are all on one side of the water, and the lions and most all the servigous creatures are on the other side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale LVIII, ending (1883); not verbatim.

title.en: The Night before Christmas: the Quarter's Lightwood Fire
title.zh: 聖誕前夜：棚戶的松明大火

region.zh: 美國喬治亞中部種植園棚戶區

texts.period: African-American festival tradition; recorded in frame narrative, published 2024 (published 1883)

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus' (2024 print of 1883), tale LXXI 'The Night before Christmas' (frame narrative)

summary.en: The holiday celebration that frames the final tales: Daddy Jack's high-hat wedding to 'Tildy, the waggon-loads of resinous lightwood heaped round the dancing platform and set ablaze at nightfall, the fiddle put away at Uncle Remus's command in favor of 'ole times', and the old man — captain of the corn-pile, stoutest at the log-rolling, swiftest with the hoe — joining one round of the dance for old times' sake with the little boy watching from the platform corner.
summary.zh: 收束全書的節慶場景：傑克老爹戴高帽迎娶蒂爾迪；載滿松明的推車環繞舞臺堆起，夜幕落下即舉火；雷慕斯老人一聲令下收起提琴，改跳『老時光的舞』——他曾是玉米堆的首領、滾木賽的壯漢、鋤地最快的快手——此刻為了舊日情誼，帶著從舞臺角上觀望的小男孩跳上一圈。

sensitivity.note: Frame-narrative festival scene (Christmas in the quarters with lightwood fires and the ring-dance), recorded by Harris as the setting for the last tales; historical depiction of antebellum-era holiday practice from a formerly enslaved teller's world, included as documentary folk material.

passages.text: The little boy had a special invitation to be present at the marriage of Daddy Jack and 'Tildy, and went accompanied by Uncle Remus and Aunt Tempy. 'Tildy wore a white dress and a wreath of artificial flowers in her hair; Daddy Jack wore a high hat, which he persisted in keeping on his head during the ceremony, and a coat the tails of which nearly dragged the floor; his bright little eyes glistened triumphantly, and he grinned and bowed to everybody again and again. After it was all over the guests partook of cake baked by Aunt Tempy and persimmon beer brewed by Uncle Remus — and 'Tildy allowed that if everything did not go right down the country with her ole man, she was going to pick up and come right back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale LXXI frame (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: The preparations for the holidays went on: a large platform used for sunning wheat and seed cotton was arranged by the negroes for their dance, and several waggon-loads of resinous pine — known as lightwood — were placed around about it in little heaps, so that the occasion might lack no element of brilliancy. At nightfall the heaps of lightwood were set on fire, and the little boy, waiting impatiently for Uncle Remus to come for him, could hear the negroes singing, dancing, and laughing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale LXXI frame, middle (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Uncle Remus came he declined the River-place fiddle — 'she sets my toof on aidje; let's go back to ole times' — and, greeting the crowd ('I just come up to join in with you for one round, for the sake of ole times, if no mo''), he stood smiling upon the crowd of negroes, picturesque in the extreme, seeming taller than all the rest and moving with all the vigor of youth: he had always exercised authority over his fellow-servants — he had been the captain of the corn-pile, the stoutest at the log-rolling, the swiftest with the hoe, the neatest with the plough, and the plantation hands still looked upon him as their leader.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale LXXI frame, ending (1883); not verbatim.
